content: Bedaquiline has been associated with significantly fewer episodes of treatment failure, relapse, and death. At the time of earlier studies, there was limited experience with its use in children under six years of age. However, its use in adolescents, patients with extrapulmonary tuberculosis (EPTB), and individuals living with HIV was increasing. Previous recommendations for longer treatment regimens suggested that bedaquiline could be included for patients aged 6–17 years. Consequently, an all-oral regimen containing bedaquiline was conditionally recommended for eligible children and adolescents aged six years and above. The recommendations for children were based on extrapolated efficacy data from adults, combined with pharmacokinetic (PK) and safety data from phase II trials in children aged 6–17 years. However, no recommendation could be made for children under six years due to a lack of evidence, particularly regarding PK, safety, and tolerability. The shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimen included medicines that had been part of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) regimens for years in both adults and children. Adverse drug reactions associated with these medicines were well-documented, and dosages were established. However, this was not the case for bedaquiline at the time of the 2019 WHO Guideline Development Group (GDG) meeting on drug-resistant TB (DR-TB). The use of bedaquiline in young children for both shorter and longer regimens was identified as a gap to be addressed in the 2021 update of the child and adolescent TB guidelines. To address the question of bedaquiline use in children under six years, data from two phase II trials (TMC207-C211 and IMPAACT P1108) were reviewed. The TMC207-C211 trial included children aged 5–18 years, while the IMPAACT P1108 trial included children aged 0–6 years. The review of PK and safety data focused primarily on the IMPAACT P1108 trial. Although the interim data sample size was small (N=12), the GDG concluded that cardiac safety signals in children aged 0–6 years were not distinct from those reported in adults. Population PK models from both studies suggested that drug exposures observed in adults could be achieved in most children receiving bedaquiline, though dose adjustments might be necessary based on age and weight. Additionally, data from a pediatric MDR/RR-TB individual patient dataset (IPD) were analyzed descriptively, including 24,231 records from all six WHO regions, with the majority from India and South Africa. A matched analysis of treatment outcomes in children treated for DR-TB included 40 children under six years and 68 children aged 6–12 years who received bedaquiline. The analysis showed that bedaquiline was significantly associated with shorter treatment durations and a lower adjusted odds ratio for injectable TB drug use. A child-friendly formulation of bedaquiline (20 mg scored uncoated tablet) is being used in the Janssen C211 study for children under five years and will soon be used in an updated protocol of the IMPAACT P1108 study. No head-to-head studies have been conducted to examine the bioequivalence of the 20 mg and 100 mg formulations of bedaquiline. However, indirect bioequivalence testing showed that both tablets have the same bioavailability and can be used interchangeably at the same total dose. Findings from the bedaquiline crush study also demonstrated that the bioavailability of bedaquiline tablets suspended in water was equivalent to that of tablets swallowed whole. The GDG discussed the desirable effects of including bedaquiline in all-oral regimens for children, noting that such regimens are more childand family-friendly, with shorter durations. The IPD analysis showed that bedaquiline-containing regimens were usually shorter than those without bedaquiline. The GDG rated the desirable effects as moderate. The main concern was the lack of data on long-term safety and adverse events. However, clinical experience with bedaquiline in young children indicated that the drug is well-tolerated, often better than in adults. Therefore, the GDG agreed that the undesirable effects were small. Overall, the GDG determined that the balance between desirable and undesirable effects likely favors the use of bedaquiline in children under six years. The GDG highlighted that the benefits may vary depending on specific contexts and population characteristics, such as nutritional status. For children living with HIV, while the TMC207-C211 trial has not yet enrolled HIV-positive children, the IMPAACT P1108 study includes both HIV-infected and uninfected infants, children, and adolescents with MDR-TB. In the pediatric IPD, 30% of children under six years treated with a bedaquiline-containing regimen were HIV-positive, compared to 20% treated with DR-TB regimens not including bedaquiline. Treatment regimens for MDR/RR-TB generally do not differ substantially for people living with HIV, and bedaquiline may be used in all children regardless of HIV status. Known drug-drug interactions, such as between bedaquiline and efavirenz, should be avoided. The shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimen is contraindicated in children with extrapulmonary forms of TB other than TB lymphadenopathy. These children should be treated with longer regimens composed of medicines from groups A, B, and C. Data on the penetration of bedaquiline across the blood-brain barrier are sparse. The removal of the age restriction for bedaquiline use means that children of all ages with confirmed MDR/RR-TB and without fluoroquinolone resistance may be offered the shorter all-oral regimen with bedaquiline if they meet the eligibility criteria. This regimen includes bedaquiline (used for six months) in combination with levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, ethionamide, ethambutol, high-dose isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and clofazimine for four months (extendable to six months if the patient remains sputum smear-positive at the end of four months), followed by five months of treatment with levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, clofazimine, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide. Children not eligible for the shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimen may benefit from individualized longer treatment regimens based on drug susceptibility patterns and the extent of TB disease. Shortening the total treatment duration to less than 18 months may be considered in children without extensive disease. Children diagnosed with rifampicin resistance only, without further drug susceptibility testing, could be treated with available bedaquiline-containing regimens at the discretion of the treating clinician. Guidance on constructing optimal all-oral treatment regimens for children with MDR/RR-TB who are not eligible for the shorter regimen is provided in the operational handbook, considering their age, resistance patterns, and extent of TB disease. The construction of these regimens aligns with WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis treatment. Evidence assessed by the GDG in November 2019 supported the safe use of bedaquiline beyond six months in people with TB who received appropriate schedules of baseline and follow-up monitoring. However, the GDG could not assess the relative effectiveness of prolonged bedaquiline use due to limited evidence and potential residual confounding in the data. If bedaquiline is stopped at six months, the regimen must include at least three effective agents. If one of the three remaining agents needs to be stopped due to toxicity, it must be replaced with a medicine from group B or group C, depending on the patient’s circumstances. The concurrent use of bedaquiline and delamanid was not supported by sufficient evidence to make a statement about its effectiveness. However, safety data assessed in 2019 suggested no additional safety concerns with the concurrent use of these medicines. Appropriate safety monitoring schedules, including ECG and electrolyte monitoring, should be in place for patients receiving these medicines. Efforts to implement child-friendly DR-TB regimens, including bedaquiline, should be accompanied by increased efforts at the country level to close the case detection gap. Evidence-based, integrated treatment decision algorithms specific to different settings should be widely implemented to ensure that MDR/RR-TB is detected and effectively treated among children. Dosing guidance for bedaquiline use in children under six years is provided in the operational handbook, based on expert consultation. The child-friendly formulation of bedaquiline (20 mg scored tablet) approved by the US FDA in May 2020 is available and can be taken whole or dispersed in water. This formulation has been included in the 8th WHO Essential Medicine List for Children. If the 20 mg formulation is unavailable, the crushed 100 mg formulation may be used.
